hints: Sort the three compounds by type first, acyl chloride, primary halogenoalkane and chlorobenzene, and recall which type reacts violently with cold water and which does not react at all.
Think about the carbon attached to Cl in each case, how electron withdrawing or donating groups and overlap with a pi system change its partial positive charge.

Link the strength and character of the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond to ease of attack by water, consider delocalisation in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ and the extra electron deficiency in $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$.
walkthrough:
Picture the three different C-Cl environments**
You have three very different situations. $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ is an acyl chloride with $\text{C(=O)-Cl}$. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ is a simple primary chloroalkane. $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ has Cl joined directly to a benzene ring. Hydrolysis means water acting as a nucleophile to replace Cl by OH, so anything that makes the C more positive and easier to attack speeds it up.

Why chlorobenzene is inert**
In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$, the p orbital on Cl containing a lone pair overlaps sideways with the delocalised pi system of the ring. That pumps electron density into the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond, giving it partial double bond character. It is shorter and stronger, and the carbon is less electron deficient, so water cannot break it under normal conditions.

Why the acyl chloride is fastest**
In $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$, the carbon bonded to Cl is also bonded to highly electronegative oxygen in $\text{C=O}$. Oxygen pulls electrons away strongly, leaving that carbon very $\delta+$. Water is attracted very strongly, the tetrahedral intermediate forms easily, and the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond there is the weakest of the three, so $\text{Cl}^-$ leaves rapidly.

Place the chloroalkane in the middle**
$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ has only a polar single $\text{C-Cl}$ bond with no extra withdrawal and no delocalisation. The ethyl group actually pushes electrons toward C by the positive inductive effect, slightly strengthening the bond compared with the acyl chloride, but it is still a normal sigma bond that water can break slowly on warming. Hence the order $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl} > \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} > \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$.

Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl} > \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} > \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ in rate of hydrolysis.
In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ the lone pair on Cl overlaps with the benzene pi system, giving the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond partial double bond character so no hydrolysis.
In $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ the carbonyl O makes the carbonyl C strongly $\delta+$, so attack by water is very easy and the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is weakest; in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ the alkyl group donates electrons and strengthens the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond relative to the acyl chloride.

hints: Remember a base is defined by protons, and weak means incomplete reaction with water, so combine those two ideas.
walkthrough:
Combine the two words**
Base tells you the chemistry: a species that accepts $\text{H}^+$ using a lone pair on N. Weak tells you the extent: in water only a small fraction of molecules accept a proton, so the equilibrium $\text{B} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{BH}^+ + \text{OH}^-$ lies far to the left.
Final answer: A proton acceptor that is only partially ionised in aqueous solution.

hints: Look for the lone pairs on the two N atoms in epibatidine and think what $\text{HCl}$ supplies to them.
walkthrough:
Spot the basic centres**
Epibatidine has a pyridine N with a lone pair in an $sp^2$ orbital and a secondary aliphatic amine $\text{>NH}$ with a lone pair. Both can accept $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{HCl(aq)}$ to form $\text{>N}^+\text{-H}$ and $\text{>NH}_2^+$.

Draw the salt**
Add $\text{H}^+$ to the N atoms, put a positive charge on each N, and show $\text{Cl}^-$ ions alongside to balance charge. In full protonation you get the dication plus $2\text{Cl}^-$. The mark scheme allows showing protonation at either N with the other left neutral, provided charges and $\text{Cl}^-$ are correct.

Final answer: Both N atoms protonated to give $\text{N}^+-\text{H}$ on the pyridine ring and $\text{NH}_2^+$ on the bridged amine, with $2\text{Cl}^-$ as counter ions. Accept either singly protonated form with $\text{Cl}^-$ if one N shown as $\text{N}^+-\text{H}$ or $\text{NH}_2^+$ and the other N neutral.

hints: Recall the two stages for $\text{RCOCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$: water adds to $\text{C=O}$ then $\text{HCl}$ is eliminated, and track what happens to the $\text{C=O}$ pi bond in each stage.
walkthrough:
Follow the carbonyl through addition then elimination**
In step 1 water attacks the $\text{C=O}$ carbon, the $\text{C=O}$ pi bond breaks to give a tetrahedral intermediate while new $\text{C-O}$ sigma bonds form. In step 2 the $\text{C=O}$ pi bond reforms as $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{H}^+$ leave. Over the whole mechanism you have broken a $\text{C-Cl}$ sigma bond and a $\text{C=O}$ pi bond, and formed a $\text{C-O}$ sigma bond and a $\text{C=O}$ pi bond. So both rows are both $\sigma$ and $\pi$.
Final answer: Bonds broken: both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds. Bonds formed: both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds.

hints: Identify the two reacting groups in $\text{H}_2\text{N-(CH}_2\text{)}_5\text{-C(=O)Cl}$ and remember $\text{-NH}_2 + \text{-COCl}$ gives $\text{-CONH-}$ plus $\text{HCl}$.
Join two monomers head to tail so the amide $\text{-C(=O)-N(H)-}$ is fully displayed, and repeat the $(\text{CH}_2)_5$ chain on each side.
walkthrough:
Make the amide link**
The amine end of one monomer attacks the acyl chloride end of the next: $$\text{-NH}_2 + \text{ClC(=O)-} \rightarrow \text{-NH-C(=O)-} + \text{HCl}$$ Draw the link fully displayed, that is $\text{C}$ double bonded to $\text{O}$ and single bonded to $\text{N}$, with $\text{H}$ shown on $\text{N}$.

Double it to show two repeats**
Nylon-6 from this monomer has the repeating sequence $\text{-NH-(CH}_2\text{)}_5\text{-CO-}$. Write it twice end to end: $$\text{-NH-(CH}_2\text{)}_5\text{-C(=O)-NH-(CH}_2\text{)}_5\text{-C(=O)-}$$ with free bonds at the ends to show continuation of the chain.

Final answer: $\text{-N(H)-(CH}_2\text{)}_5\text{-C(=O)-N(H)-(CH}_2\text{)}_5\text{-C(=O)-}$ with amide bonds fully displayed as $\text{-C(=O)-N(H)-}$, continuation bonds at each end, two repeat units shown.

hints: Split the six-carbon backbone shown into two alkene units by pairing adjacent carbons, look for the repeating two-carbon pattern of addition polymerisation.
Reverse polymerisation by replacing each $\text{C-C}$ single bond between monomer units with a $\text{C=C}$ double bond and restoring the substituents to each $\text{C}$.
walkthrough:
Read the polymer section in pairs**
Addition polymers are made by opening $\text{C=C}$ to $\text{C-C}$. To go backwards, cut the long $\text{C-C}$ chain into two-carbon alkene pieces. The section shows alternating substitution patterns that fit two different monomers combining.

Reform the double bonds**
Take one pair to give $\text{H}_2\text{C=CHC}_2\text{H}_5$ where the two carbons carry $\text{CH}_3,\text{Cl}$ and $\text{H},\text{H}$ in the polymer becoming $\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{CH}$ in the monomer. Take the other block to give $\text{H}_3\text{CCH=C(CH}_3\text{)Cl}$ where the polymer carbons carrying $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5,\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_3,\text{H}$ plus the next $\text{CH}_3,\text{Cl}$ and $\text{H},\text{H}$ regroup to the substituted butene. Either consistent pairing that accounts for all substituents is accepted.

Final answer: $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (but-1-ene) and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=C(CH}_3\text{)Cl}$ (2-chlorobut-2-ene). Allow the alternative pairing: $\text{CH}_3\text{CCl=CH}_2$ (2-chloropropene) and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH=CHCH}_3$ (pent-2-ene).

hints: Compare the backbone bonds, polar $\text{C-N}$ and $\text{C=O}$ in a polyamide versus non-polar $\text{C-C}$ in a polyalkene, and think which can be attacked by water or enzymes.
walkthrough:
Link polarity to attack by water**
Biodegradation usually needs hydrolysis by water or enzymes. The polyalkene backbone is just non-polar $\text{C-C}$ and $\text{C-H}$ bonds with no partial charges, so water has nowhere to attack. The polyamide has the polar $\text{-CONH-}$ group with $\delta+$ C that is readily hydrolysed back to carboxylic acid and amine, breaking the chain.
Final answer: $\text{C-C}$ bonds in polyalkenes are non-polar and cannot be hydrolysed, whereas polyamides contain polar amide links that can be broken down by hydrolysis.

hints: Look at the change from phenylethanone in step 1 to phenylethene after step 3, step 2 must lower the carbonyl to an alcohol that can then dehydrate.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from the alkene**
Phenylethene is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=CH}_2$ made by dehydration in step 3, so H must be the alcohol that dehydrates to it. Reduction of the ketone $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$ adds two H across $\text{C=O}$ to give the secondary alcohol $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$.
Final answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$, 1-phenylethan-1-ol.

hints: Step 1 adds a $\text{CH}_3\text{C=O}$ group to benzene, recall the electrophile and Lewis acid catalyst needed for acylation of benzene.
Step 2 converts a ketone to a secondary alcohol without affecting the benzene ring, think of mild hydride reducing agents.
Step 3 converts the alcohol H to the alkene phenylethene, recall the dehydrating agent and heating used to eliminate water.
walkthrough:
Acylate benzene to the methyl ketone**
Benzene to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$ is Friedel-Crafts acylation. The electrophile comes from ethanoyl chloride with the Lewis acid catalyst aluminium chloride: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{CH}_3\text{COCl} \xrightarrow{\text{AlCl}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3 + \text{HCl}$$

Reduce the ketone to the alcohol**
Ketone to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ needs hydride addition. Use sodium tetrahydridoborate $\text{NaBH}_4$ in methanol or lithium aluminium hydride $\text{LiAlH}_4$ in dry ether, followed by dilute acid work up. This does not reduce the benzene ring.

Dehydrate to the alkene**
Alcohol to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=CH}_2$ is elimination of water. Heat with concentrated sulfuric acid, which protonates OH to leave as $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and forms the $\text{C=C}$ bond: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(OH)CH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4, \text{heat}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=CH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
